title: The Owner Leads Through a System, Not Through Presence
summary: An owner does not lead a construction project by being on site or by being forceful. Marco, with Kema, teaches the five parts of an owner's operating system, authority, cadence, escalation, accountability and, as the last rung, termination, and how each one keeps decisions fast and defensible.
body:
An owner leads a project through a small operating system, who may decide what, how often people meet, how disagreements climb and who owns each action, and the system has to be built before the first difficult week, because it cannot be improvised during one.

Recall

Q. What is an ipso facto clause, and why can it fail?

A. A clause allowing termination because a party becomes insolvent. Insolvency law, including United States bankruptcy law, can restrict enforcing it, so owners usually terminate for failure to perform after proper notice instead.

Q. What are the four passes for reading a finished building?

A. Structure, systems, sequence and cost, in that order, looking for the early decisions that drove the rest.

Q. Why do steel shop drawings matter to the owner?

A. Because connections are often finalised in shop drawings, and a change made there must be reviewed by the responsible engineer; otherwise a detail can change without anyone who understands its load checking it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Kema joins me this week because leading as owner is half technical and half human. You come from shift operations, where authority is written down, handovers are structured and escalation follows a procedure. That is a real advantage. Many developers run projects on personality: they visit site, make decisions in corridors and expect loyalty. It works until the first week when everyone is under pressure at once. Then decisions stall, contradict each other or are made by whoever happens to be present.

Kema adds the human half. A system protects people as much as it controls them. A site representative who knows his limit can say "that is above my authority, I will have an answer by Thursday" without losing face. A contractor who knows the escalation clock does not need to shout to be heard. And you, as owner, can rest on a day off knowing that decisions within the matrix are being made properly without you. Leadership that depends on your presence fails the first night you are on shift.

Authority: who may decide what

Plain English first. Every decision on a project belongs to someone. If nobody has written down who, the contractor will ask whoever is easiest to persuade. The professional tool is a delegation of authority matrix: a table listing types of decision, the value limits, and the person who may approve each, with who must be consulted first.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Your matrix might say: the owner's site representative may approve changes up to 10,000 dollars with no effect on time, structure, fire or accessibility. The project manager may approve up to 50,000 dollars and up to 5 days of time. Anything above that, any change to structure, fire protection, egress or accessibility, any change to the completion date and any use of contingency above a stated amount comes to you, with the responsible designer's written advice. The matrix goes to the contractor and the design team at the start, so that they know an instruction from anyone else does not bind you. That last point is legal as well as practical; LEX covers it on Day 4.

Cadence: how often, and for what

Cadence is the rhythm of meetings, and each meeting needs a purpose. A common pattern is a weekly meeting of owner, architect and contractor, often called the OAC meeting, for progress, requests for information, submittals, changes and the next three weeks of work. A monthly principals' meeting, where the senior people of each firm review cost, schedule, risk and the relationship. And a monthly or quarterly report to your lender and investors. The daily coordination on site belongs to the contractor; an owner who attends every daily huddle soon becomes the person everyone waits for.

The rules that make cadence work are simple. A written agenda and the key reports circulate a day ahead. Decisions are recorded in the meeting, not afterwards from memory. Every action has one name and one date. And the meeting ends on time.

Say that out loud now.

Authority written down, a fixed cadence, one name and one date on every action.

Escalation and accountability

Escalation is the route a disagreement climbs when the people closest to it cannot resolve it. A good ladder has time limits on each rung, so that disputes move instead of festering. For example: the project team has 5 working days; if unresolved, the principals have 10; if still unresolved, the contract's dispute process begins. Accountability is the record that shows who agreed to do what, by when, and whether they did. The owner's decision log, taught in Week 48, is its core.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A request for information on the critical path, the chain of activities that sets the completion date, needs a design answer within the contract's 5 working days. Your architect is slow and the answer arrives on day 15. The project has lost 10 working days of float, or of completion date if no float existed. At a hypothetical carry of 15,000 dollars a working day for interest and overheads, that is 150,000 dollars. An escalation rule that brought it to the principals on day 6 would have cost one phone call. Late owner-side decisions are among the commonest causes of compensable delay, and they are yours.

Termination: the last rung

Termination of a contractor is the final rung of the ladder, not a separate decision. It is legitimate only when the earlier rungs have been used and documented: notices given, cure periods allowed, meetings recorded. An owner who has run a clean cadence has that record without trying. An owner who has run the project on phone calls discovers, at the worst moment, that the evidence does not exist. Ford's Day 2 case shows what that costs.

How the best do it

Owners who run large capital programmes well tend to share a few habits, whatever their size. They publish the authority matrix and enforce it, so that a contractor who acts on an unauthorised instruction does so at its own risk. They run an unchanging meeting rhythm with pre-reads and a live decision log, and they review a short dashboard of the same few measures every month: cost to complete, schedule float, open changes, open hold points and safety. And they separate the relationship meeting from the progress meeting, so that tensions between principals do not consume the weekly coordination. A small developer can copy every one of these with a spreadsheet and a calendar.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: who signs and approves costs affects the evidence behind what is capitalised or deducted; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an instruction from someone without authority may still bind you if the contractor reasonably relied on it. Banking: lenders read your reporting cadence as a sign of control. Governance: the authority matrix should be approved by your company's board or owners and match its resolutions. Estate: a project run on a written system can continue if you cannot; one run on your presence cannot. Exit: clean decision records shorten due diligence when you sell or refinance.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on how the authority matrix and notice provisions fit the contract.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is decision by presence: whoever is on site decides, so instructions conflict, authority is unclear and the record is thin. The control is the authority matrix, issued at award and enforced from the first week.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that being on site every day is leadership. It often makes you the bottleneck. Lead through the system, and visit to observe and to check that the system is working.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the project charter, governance, approval authorities and the owner decision log. Those were the plans. This week they become behaviour under pressure: the charter only matters if the matrix is enforced on the morning a contractor wants a quick yes.

Recap

Lead through five parts: written authority, a fixed cadence, an escalation ladder with time limits, accountability through one name and one date per action, and termination as the documented last rung. Build it before the first hard week.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a termination that cost more than the contractor.
checklist: I issue a delegation of authority matrix to the contractor and designers at award.
I state that instructions from anyone outside the matrix do not bind me.
I run a weekly owner-architect-contractor meeting with a pre-read circulated a day ahead.
I hold a monthly principals' meeting separate from the progress meeting.
I record decisions during the meeting, with one name and one date on every action.
I use an escalation ladder with time limits on each rung.
I track owner-side decision times, especially on critical-path questions.
I treat termination as the last documented rung, never a separate decision.
head: Field checklist
speak: An owner leads a project through a system, not through presence. Five parts. Authority: a written matrix showing who may approve which decisions up to which value, with structure, fire, egress, accessibility and the completion date reserved to the owner. Cadence: a weekly owner-architect-contractor meeting, a monthly principals' meeting and regular reports to lenders and investors, each with a pre-read, live decisions and one name and one date on every action. Escalation: a ladder with time limits, such as five working days for the project team and ten for the principals before the contract's dispute process. Accountability: the decision and action logs. And termination as the last documented rung. In a hypothetical case, a critical-path design answer ten days late cost 150,000 dollars; an escalation rule would have cost a phone call. Build the system before the first hard week.
terms: Delegation of authority matrix — a table setting out which person may approve each type and value of decision, and who must be consulted first.
OAC meeting — the regular meeting of owner, architect and contractor to manage progress, information requests, submittals and changes.
Escalation ladder — a defined sequence of levels, each with a time limit, through which an unresolved disagreement rises.

hostile.q: Your site representative approved a 40,000 dollar change last week. Your own matrix says his limit is 10,000. Is that change approved or not?
hostile.a: Not by me, and we have told the contractor so in writing. The matrix was issued at award and states that instructions beyond a person's limit do not bind the owner. We are reviewing the change on its merits through the normal route this week; if it is justified, I will approve it properly, and if it is not, the contractor acted on an instruction it knew was outside his authority. I have also spoken to the representative. The matrix only protects us if we enforce it every time.

title: The Termination That Cost More Than the Contractor: A Composite
summary: A composite case: an owner, frustrated by a slow contractor, terminated for default without completing the contract's notice and cure steps, after months of instructions given outside the authority matrix. The termination was found wrongful, and the owner paid the replacement premium and the original contractor's lost profit together.
body:
This is a composite example. An owner terminated a slow contractor in anger, skipped the contract's notice and cure steps and had a file full of informal instructions; the termination was held wrongful, and the owner paid twice for the same building.

Recall

Q. After a contractor default, where does the cost-to-complete calculation start?

A. From independently verified work in place, never from the contractor's last pay application.

Q. State Rule 120.

A. Never adopt a benchmark cycle time until its crane, formwork, labour, concrete and inspection system is matched, and never strip or reshore on the calendar; strip only on in-place strength the engineer of record has approved.

Q. What does erection stability mean for a steel frame?

A. Keeping a partly erected frame stable, with temporary bracing and a planned sequence, until the permanent connections, floors and lateral system are complete.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole sits with me today because this failure was decided by documents. The owner in this case was not wrong that the contractor was slow. He was wrong about what he could prove and about what the contract required before he acted. Termination is the most powerful remedy an owner has and the easiest one to lose. This is a composite example, assembled from patterns that recur in construction disputes. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

A developer signs a 20,000,000 dollar contract for a hypothetical mid-rise residential building. By month 6, progress is behind and the owner is irritated. From month 6 to month 9, he and his site manager, who has no authority under the contract, give the contractor a series of verbal instructions: resequence the floors, change the kitchen layout on half the units, add a temporary access road. The contractor complies and logs the instructions. In month 10, the owner sends an email: "Your performance is unacceptable. You are terminated effective Friday." He bars the contractor from site, engages a replacement and withholds the last payment. The contractor claims wrongful termination. An arbitrator, about 18 months later, finds that the contract's notice and cure requirements were not met and that much of the delay was caused by the owner's own instructions.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Giving instructions through someone without authority, outside the change process. Not issuing formal notices of default when performance first slipped, so no cure period ever started. And terminating by email in a single step, out of frustration, without legal review.

3. Assumptions

The owner assumed that because the contractor was slow, termination for default was obviously justified. He assumed his informal instructions had not affected the schedule, because he thought of them as small. He assumed that an email from the owner was a valid notice. And he assumed that a tribunal would judge the contractor's performance, when in practice it judged the owner's compliance with the contract first.

4. Incentives

The site manager wanted to look helpful and gave instructions to keep work moving. The contractor had every incentive to comply and record each instruction, because each was a potential claim for time and money. The owner wanted speed and control. Only the contractor was building a file.

Say that out loud now.

A termination is won or lost in the paper written months before it.

5. Warning signs ignored

The contractor's monthly reports began listing "owner instructions" as a cause of delay in month 7. Requests for change orders to formalise the verbal instructions went unanswered. The schedule updates showed the critical path running through the resequenced floors. The owner's lawyer, when copied once in month 8, recommended a formal notice and a meeting; the advice was not followed.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the email in month 10, followed by barring the contractor from site. Up to then the owner could have issued a proper notice of default, allowed the cure period, regularised the instructions as changes and, if performance did not improve, terminated with a clean record. After the email, the owner had repudiated the contract on a defective notice, and the question was only how much it would cost.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not the contractor's slowness. It was running the project outside its own system: no authority matrix enforced, no change process for owner instructions and no formal notices. When the owner reached for the last rung of the ladder, the rungs below it did not exist.

Cole's view: what the tribunal read

Cole reads the file as the tribunal did. The contract required written notice of default specifying the failures, a stated cure period and, in this form, a certification by the owner's consultant that sufficient cause existed. None was given. The contractor's logs showed dated owner instructions that had not been processed as changes, and its schedule analysis linked them to most of the delay. The owner's email named no specific failure. Many contracts provide that a termination for default later found invalid is treated as a termination for convenience; this one did, so the owner owed the contractor its costs and a margin on the work not performed. Verify how your own contract and law treat wrongful termination before you rely on any of this.

What it cost

Worked example, hypothetical. The replacement contractor finished the remaining 9,000,000 dollars of work for 11,000,000 dollars, a premium of 2,000,000. The owner paid the original contractor the 600,000 dollars it had withheld, which was owed in any event, 1,200,000 dollars for the unprocessed instructions as changes and 700,000 dollars for lost margin and demobilisation under the convenience conversion. Legal and expert costs came to about 800,000 dollars, most of it borne by the owner. Delay added 5 months at 180,000 dollars a month, 900,000 dollars. Above the original contract sum, that is 2,000,000 plus 1,200,000 plus 700,000 plus 800,000 plus 900,000, about 5,600,000 dollars. The changes might have been priced anyway; the other 4,400,000 dollars, the premium, lost margin, legal costs and delay, flowed from the termination itself, and two letters and a change log would have avoided most of it.

What a clean termination looks like

Run the same facts the right way. In month 6, the owner issues a formal notice of default, naming the failures against the baseline schedule and the staffing commitments, and allowing the contract's cure period. In the same week, he processes the access road and resequencing as written changes, priced and with time assessed, so that the contractor's slowness is separated from the owner's own effect on the schedule. During the cure period, the principals meet weekly and the minutes record what was promised and delivered. If the contractor recovers, the project continues with a better relationship than before. If it does not, counsel reviews the file, the consultant certifies cause where the form requires it, the surety is notified under the bond, and the termination notice cites specific, documented failures. The contractor may still dispute it, but now the owner is defending a record rather than an email.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, before any notice of default or termination is issued.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is terminating on frustration rather than on a documented record. The control is a rule that no termination step is taken without counsel reading the file, the contract's notice and cure steps completed and the owner's own instructions reconciled first.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking of notices as hostile. A formal notice of default, issued early and calmly, is often what turns a slow contractor around, and if it does not, it is what makes the termination valid.

Callback

In Week 81, LEX taught the dispute ladder and the limitation periods that govern it, and in Week 118 Marco and Petra taught notice and time bars. This case runs the same rules against the owner: the contractor gave its notices and kept its records, and the owner did neither.

Recap

An owner gave informal instructions outside the authority matrix, never issued formal notices and terminated by email. The termination was found wrongful and converted to convenience, and the owner paid the replacement premium, the unprocessed changes and the contractor's lost margin together.

Rule 122: Never terminate a contractor until the contract's notice, cure and certification steps are complete and documented, your own instructions are reconciled as changes and counsel has read the file; a termination is won or lost in the paper written months before it.

Next: Roman on The Money: what slow decisions and a bad termination cost.
checklist: I never give or allow instructions outside the authority matrix.
I process every owner instruction as a written change, promptly.
I issue a formal notice of default early, specifying the failures, when performance slips.
I allow the contract's cure period in full and document what happened during it.
I complete any required certification before a termination step.
I have counsel read the whole file before any termination.
I reconcile my own instructions and delays before I judge the contractor's.
I never bar a contractor from site or withhold payment without legal advice.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. An owner frustrated by a slow contractor let his site manager, who had no authority, give months of verbal instructions: resequencing floors, changing kitchens, adding an access road. None were processed as changes. No formal notice of default was ever issued, so no cure period started. Then the owner terminated by email, barred the contractor and withheld payment. The tribunal found the notice and cure steps had not been met and much of the delay was the owner's. Under the contract, the wrongful termination was treated as one for convenience, so the owner paid the replacement premium, the unprocessed changes and the contractor's lost margin together, more than 5 million dollars above the original contract sum. Rule 122: never terminate until notice, cure and certification are complete, your instructions are reconciled and counsel has read the file.
terms: Notice of default — a formal written notice telling a contractor which obligations it has failed to meet and what it must do, often starting a cure period.
Cure period — the time a contract allows a party in default to correct its failure before the other party may terminate.
Termination for convenience — ending a contract without fault on the other side, usually on payment of work done, costs and sometimes a margin.

hostile.q: The contractor was months behind. Why should you pay it anything after you terminated?
hostile.a: Because the termination did not meet the contract. We issued no formal notice of default, allowed no cure period and skipped the required certification, and our own site manager had given instructions that were never processed as changes and that caused much of the delay. The contract treats a defective termination for default as one for convenience. I accept that and the cost it brings. What I have changed is the system: an enforced authority matrix, a change log for every owner instruction, and counsel's review before any notice is sent.

rule: Rule 122: Never terminate a contractor until the contract's notice, cure and certification steps are complete and documented, your own instructions are reconciled as changes and counsel has read the file; a termination is won or lost in the paper written months before it.

title: The Price of Slow Decisions and the Price of Getting Rid of a Contractor
summary: Roman prices two things owners rarely put a number on: the cost of their own decision latency, and the cost of each option for dealing with a failing contractor, from a remedial plan to a negotiated exit to termination. Expected values show why the cheapest-looking option is often the most expensive.
body:
An owner's slow decision costs money by the working day, and the choice of how to deal with a failing contractor is a priced decision between options with very different expected costs; both deserve numbers before they deserve opinions.

Recall

Q. What is a lien waiver?

A. A signed release by a subcontractor or supplier of its right to claim against the property for work already paid.

Q. What is the efficiency ratio of a floor plate?

A. Net saleable or rentable area divided by gross floor area.

Q. What is a moment connection in a steel frame?

A. A connection designed to transfer bending as well as shear between a beam and a column, which makes it stiffer and more expensive than a simple shear connection.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, lenders watch two things during construction that are under the owner's direct control: how fast you decide and how you handle trouble with the contractor. Both show up in the in-balance test. A slow owner burns interest reserve. A bad termination creates a funding gap. Neither is visible in a pro forma, which is exactly why I want them priced.

The price of decision latency

Plain English first. Decision latency is the time between a question reaching the owner and the owner answering it. Most of it costs nothing, because most questions are not on the critical path. The few that are cost the project's daily carry for every day of delay they cause.

The professional framing is the daily cost of delay: interest on the drawn loan, the contractor's time-related costs, or general conditions, if the delay is compensable, and your own overheads. Week 118 taught when delay is compensable. Here we only count what it costs.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A project has 14,000,000 dollars drawn on a construction loan at a hypothetical 8 percent. Daily interest is 14,000,000 times 0.08 divided by 365, about 3,068 dollars. The contractor's general conditions run 9,000 dollars a working day and the owner's overheads 2,000. If a critical-path delay is owner-caused and compensable, each working day costs about 9,000 plus 2,000 plus roughly 4,300 of interest per working day, about 15,300 dollars. Ten slow decisions a year, each costing 3 critical-path days, cost about 460,000 dollars. That is the hidden price of running a project on your availability rather than on an authority matrix.

Notice the leverage. The fix is not working harder. It is pushing decisions down to people with clear limits, and escalating the few that matter on a clock.

Setting your own decision covenant

Lenders impose covenants on you. It is worth imposing one on yourself. Write down a target turnaround for each class of owner decision, for example 3 working days for a critical-path request for information that needs an owner choice, 5 for a priced change within contingency and 10 for anything that changes the completion date, and report your actual average at the monthly principals' meeting. The number does two jobs. It tells the contractor and the design team that you take your own delays as seriously as theirs, which weakens any later claim that the owner was the bottleneck. And it tells you where your own system is failing, before a delay analysis tells a tribunal.

Worked example, hypothetical. Your log shows 40 owner decisions in a quarter, averaging 6 working days, against a target of 4. Eight of them were on the critical path. If each of those eight added 2 days that the project could not absorb, that is 16 working days at 15,300 dollars, about 245,000 dollars in a single quarter. The remedy is usually structural: raise a delegate's limit, add a standing weekly decision slot or move one class of approval to the project manager.

The price of each exit from a failing contractor

When a contractor is failing, you have roughly four options. Work with it under a written remedial plan. Negotiate an exit by agreement. Terminate for default, properly. Or, if things go wrong, end up with a wrongful termination. Each has a cost and a probability of success.

Worked example two, hypothetical, with 9,000,000 dollars of work remaining. Option A, remedial plan: you fund 300,000 dollars of acceleration and a site-based cost consultant, and you judge a 60 percent chance it works. If it fails, you terminate later, at a cost of 3,000,000 dollars above contract. Expected cost: 300,000 plus 0.4 times 3,000,000, which is 1,500,000 dollars.

Option B, negotiated exit: you pay 400,000 dollars to end the contract by agreement, with releases, assigned subcontracts and an orderly handover, and the replacement premium on the remaining work is 1,500,000 because the handover is clean. Expected cost about 1,900,000 dollars, with high certainty.

Option C, termination for default, done properly: replacement premium 2,000,000, rectification and gap costs 500,000, a 40 percent chance of a dispute costing 1,000,000, less a 50 percent chance of a 1,500,000 dollar bond recovery. Expected cost: 2,500,000 plus 400,000 less 750,000, which is 2,150,000 dollars, with wide variance.

Option D, wrongful termination, Ford's composite: about 4,400,000 dollars of avoidable cost.

Say that out loud now.

Price every exit. The cheapest-looking option is rarely the cheapest expected cost.

The numbers are hypothetical, and in a real case your probabilities will be judgments. The point is the comparison. An owner who has priced the options chooses calmly. An owner who has not chooses termination, because it feels decisive.

What the lender sees

A lender's credit committee reads each option through three questions: does the loan stay in balance, does the completion date stay inside the loan's maturity, and does the guarantee get called? A remedial plan that works keeps all three green. A clean negotiated exit usually needs a modest equity injection and a revised schedule, which a lender can approve. A contested termination creates uncertainty on all three for months. That is why lenders often prefer a planned exit to a dramatic one, and why you should talk to the lender before you choose, not after.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

The scarcest asset on your personal balance sheet during construction is not cash. It is your own time and judgment. A decision made tired, or late, has a cost you have just seen. Treat your decision capacity as a resource to protect: delegate within clear limits, keep the few critical decisions for rested hours and do not stake a guarantee on choices made in frustration. On the money side, any exit option that needs equity draws on your liquidity floor, so know before trouble starts how much you could inject without breaching it. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer and quantity surveyor, before choosing an exit from a failing contractor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing an exit on emotion, usually termination because it feels like control. The control is a one-page comparison of the options, with costs, probabilities and the lender's view, prepared with counsel and the quantity surveyor before any notice is sent.

The beginner's mistake

Treating owner decisions as free. Every critical-path question you leave in your inbox has a daily price.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught base, downside and severe cases. The exit comparison is that method applied to a single decision: each option has a base outcome and a downside, and you choose the one whose downside you can survive, not the one whose base case looks best.

Recap

Owner-caused critical-path delay costs the daily carry, about 15,300 dollars a working day in our hypothetical. A failing contractor offers four exits with very different expected costs; a negotiated exit or a properly documented termination usually beats a dramatic one. Price the options, ask the lender early and protect your own decision capacity.

Next: LEX on The Rules: authority, notice and termination, and what the contract actually lets you do.
checklist: I calculate the project's daily cost of delay and keep it on the dashboard.
I track how long critical-path questions wait for an owner decision.
I push decisions down to people with clear limits.
I price every exit option for a failing contractor before choosing one.
I assign probabilities and compare expected costs and downsides.
I talk to the lender before choosing an exit, not after.
I know how much equity I could inject without breaching my liquidity floor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two owner costs rarely get priced. The first is decision latency. In a hypothetical project with 14 million dollars drawn, interest, the contractor's general conditions and owner overheads make each owner-caused critical-path working day cost about 15,300 dollars, so ten slow decisions a year costing three days each is about 460,000 dollars. The fix is an authority matrix and an escalation clock, not working harder. The second is the exit from a failing contractor. A remedial plan, a negotiated exit, a properly documented termination and a wrongful termination each have a cost and a probability. In our example their expected costs were about 1.5, 1.9, 2.15 and 4.4 million dollars. Price the options with counsel and the quantity surveyor, ask the lender early and choose the downside you can survive, not the option that feels decisive.
terms: Decision latency — the time between a question reaching the decision-maker and the answer being given.
General conditions — the contractor's time-related site costs, such as supervision, site offices and equipment, which grow with project duration.
Negotiated exit — ending a construction contract by agreement, with payment, releases and an orderly handover, instead of by termination.

hostile.q: Your contractor is clearly failing. Why are you spending money on a remedial plan instead of terminating now?
hostile.a: Because we priced the options. A remedial plan costs about 300,000 dollars and, on our quantity surveyor's and counsel's view, has a better than even chance of working; if it fails, we terminate with a clean record, because the plan runs inside the contract's notice and cure process. Terminating now would cost a replacement premium of about 2,000,000 dollars plus a likely dispute. The expected cost of the plan is lower and its downside is a properly documented termination, which keeps the loan, the schedule and the bond position intact. We review it weekly against stated milestones.

title: Authority, Notice and Termination: What the Contract Lets You Do
summary: LEX explains the law behind leading as owner: actual and apparent authority, designated representative clauses, notice requirements, and the difference between termination for default and termination for convenience, including what happens when a termination for default is found invalid.
body:
The contract, and the law of agency behind it, decides whose instructions bind you, what a valid notice looks like and how you may end the relationship; leading as owner means acting inside those rules, especially when you are angry.

Recall

Q. What are the three failure modes of last week's post-mortem?

A. A change after sign-off that skipped its designer, a bypassed hold point and a contractor failing in plain sight, all sharing the root of a skipped control.

Q. What are instruments of service?

A. The drawings, specifications and other documents a design professional produces, commonly owned by the designer and licensed to the owner for one project under standard design agreements.

Q. Why does title to off-site work matter?

A. Because if you pay for prefabricated work stored at a supplier's yard and the supplier fails, you need clear legal title, identification and insurance, or the goods may be claimed by the supplier's creditors.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Marco built the operating system and Ford showed what happens when an owner acts outside it. My job is the legal frame underneath, so that you know which actions are safe and which create liability. None of this is a jurisdictional conclusion. Contracts and the law of each place differ, and you need a construction lawyer for any real decision.

Authority: actual and apparent

Plain English first. Agency is the legal relationship in which one person, the agent, acts for another, the principal. Week 21 introduced it. Actual authority is the authority you have really given someone, in writing or by clear instruction. Apparent authority, sometimes called ostensible authority, arises when your words or conduct lead a third party reasonably to believe that someone can act for you, even if you never gave them that power. If your site manager has given instructions for months and you have paid for the results, a contractor may argue he had apparent authority, whatever your internal rules said.

The professional framing: most construction contracts name the owner's representative and say who may issue instructions and sign changes. That clause, backed by an authority matrix sent to the contractor, narrows apparent authority, because the contractor has been told in writing whose instructions bind you. Conduct can still widen it again. If you routinely honour instructions from someone outside the clause, you may be found to have accepted them.

Worked example one, hypothetical. The contract names you as owner's representative, with the project manager as your designated alternate for changes up to 50,000 dollars. Your site manager instructs a 30,000 dollar change. The contractor performs it without querying authority. Whether you must pay depends on the contract wording, the contractor's knowledge of the limits and your conduct afterwards. If you then say nothing for two months and approve a payment that includes it, many tribunals would find you have ratified the instruction, meaning approved it after the fact. The control is to reject or regularise any unauthorised instruction in writing as soon as you learn of it.

Notice: form, content and timing

Contracts usually require notices to be in writing, delivered by stated methods to stated addresses, and some require particular content. A notice of default commonly must identify the failures, refer to the clause relied on and state the cure period. Email may or may not be a valid method under your contract; read the notices clause. An informal message that misses any of these elements may be treated as no notice at all, which is why Ford's composite owner lost.

Say that out loud now.

Whose instructions bind me, what a valid notice must say, and how it must be delivered: I read those three clauses before I need them.

Termination for default and for convenience

Termination for default, or for cause, ends the contract because the contractor has failed in a way the contract defines. Standard forms in the United States commonly require a sequence: written notice, a period to cure and, in some forms, a certification by the owner's architect or consultant that sufficient cause exists. After a valid termination, the owner may typically take over the site, materials and equipment, have the work finished by others, and recover the excess cost from the contractor or its surety. Verify the exact steps in your form and governing law.

Termination for convenience allows the owner to end the contract without fault, usually on payment for work done, costs of demobilisation and sometimes overhead and profit on work performed, and, in some forms, a fee on the remaining work. Many contracts add a conversion clause: a termination for default later found invalid is treated as a termination for convenience. That clause limits the damage of a mistake, but it also means you pay for the work you took away.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your contract contains a contingent assignment of subcontracts: on termination for default, the contractor's subcontracts are assigned to you if you accept them in writing. You terminate properly and accept the assignment of the electrical and mechanical subcontracts within the stated time. Those trades stay on site at their contract prices, and your replacement premium falls on the remaining trades only. Had you missed the acceptance deadline, you would be renegotiating with every subcontractor from a position of weakness.

Withholding, set-off and suspension

Owners under pressure often reach for the money before the contract. Withholding means not paying all or part of an amount certified or claimed; set-off means deducting from what you owe an amount you say the contractor owes you. Most contracts allow both only on defined grounds, such as defective work, unpaid subcontractors or third-party claims, and often require written notice stating the amount and the reason before the payment falls due. Some jurisdictions add prompt payment rules that restrict withholding further. Withhold without a contractual ground and the required notice, and you may give the contractor the right to suspend work for non-payment, or to treat your failure to pay as a breach. The owner then becomes the party in default. Read the payment and withholding clauses alongside the termination clause, because in a dispute they are argued together. Verify any statutory payment rules against the primary source in the governing jurisdiction.

Wrongful termination

If an owner terminates without the right to do so, or without following the required steps, the termination can be treated as a repudiation, a refusal to perform the contract, which entitles the contractor to damages, often including the profit it would have earned. That is the outcome a conversion clause is designed to soften. Barring a contractor from site or withholding sums due before termination is valid can add to the claim.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer in the governing jurisdiction, before any notice of default, termination or assignment acceptance.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is creating authority, waiving rights or repudiating the contract by your own conduct under pressure. The control is a short rule: every instruction through the matrix, every notice reviewed by counsel against the notices clause, and no termination without the full sequence documented.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that "the owner said so" is a contractual act. Under most contracts, only the right person, in the right form, at the right address, creates an obligation.

Callback

In Week 20, LEX taught formation, conditions, breach and remedies. Termination is where all four meet: the contract defines the conditions, the contractor's breach must match them, and the remedy depends on following the steps. A termination that skips a condition turns the owner's remedy into the contractor's claim.

Recap

Actual authority is what you grant; apparent authority is what your conduct implies. Name your representatives, reject or regularise unauthorised instructions and read the notices clause. Termination for default needs notice, cure and sometimes certification; a defective one may convert to convenience or become repudiation.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: working backward from the final account of a terminated contract.
checklist: I name my representatives and their limits in the contract and in writing to the contractor.
I reject or regularise any unauthorised instruction in writing as soon as I learn of it.
I read the notices clause for method, address and required content.
I have counsel review every notice of default against the clause relied on.
I follow the full termination sequence: notice, cure and any required certification.
I accept contingent assignments of key subcontracts within the stated time.
I never bar a contractor from site or withhold sums due without legal advice.
I know whether my contract converts a defective default termination to convenience.
head: Field checklist
speak: Leading as owner sits on three legal ideas. Authority: actual authority is what you really grant; apparent authority is what your conduct leads the contractor to believe, and paying for months of instructions from your site manager can create it, or ratify them after the fact. Name your representatives and limits in writing, and reject or regularise unauthorised instructions at once. Notice: contracts usually require written notice by stated methods to stated addresses, and a notice of default must identify the failures, the clause and the cure period. Termination: for default typically needs notice, cure and sometimes a consultant's certification; for convenience lets you end without fault on payment for work done and costs. A defective default termination may be converted to convenience, or treated as repudiation. Accept contingent assignments of key subcontracts on time. Verify everything with a construction lawyer.
terms: Apparent authority — authority a third party reasonably believes an agent has because of the principal's words or conduct, even if it was never granted.
Ratification — approving an unauthorised act after the fact, which makes it binding as if it had been authorised.
Contingent assignment — a contract term by which subcontracts pass to the owner on termination of the main contract, if the owner accepts them.

hostile.q: Your project manager approved a dozen changes above his limit and you paid the invoices. Now you say they were unauthorised. Which is it?
hostile.a: I accept the risk that by paying without objection we may have ratified them, and I will not argue otherwise on the ones already paid. What I have done is stop it: the contractor has written notice that only the named representatives may instruct changes within stated limits, every open instruction is being reviewed and either approved through the change process or rejected in writing this week, and our payments now go through a change log that counsel has reviewed. From here, an instruction outside the matrix is at the contractor's risk.

title: Working Backward: From a Final Account, a Walk-Away Price and a Completion Date
summary: Three reverse calculations for an owner who leads: decomposing the final account of a terminated contract into what the termination itself cost, finding the most you should pay for a negotiated exit, and working back from a completion date to the decision turnaround you must hold. All figures are hypothetical.
body:
Working backward from an outcome tells you what really drove it and what you can afford: the final account shows what a termination cost, the alternative shows your walk-away price for a negotiated exit, and the completion date sets the speed at which you must decide.

Recall

Q. What are the five parts of an owner's operating system?

A. Written authority, a fixed meeting cadence, an escalation ladder with time limits, accountability through one name and one date per action, and termination as the documented last rung.

Q. In reverse engineering a finished building, what did the gap between the best floor and the average floor represent?

A. Time lost to weather, breakdowns, inspections, supply and the learning curve; the average is what the project actually did and what you should plan on.

Q. Why is erection sequence part of steel design, not only construction?

A. Because a partly built frame can be less stable than the finished one, so the engineer and erector must agree a sequence and temporary bracing that keep it stable at every stage.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so we start from finished outcomes and work backward. An owner's decisions are easier to judge after the fact, and the trick of the professional is to do the after-the-fact arithmetic before the decision. All figures are hypothetical and round, and every probability is a judgment that would come from your lawyer and quantity surveyor in a real case.

Reverse one: decomposing a final account

The outcome: an owner's final account shows 25,600,000 dollars paid in total to finish a building whose original contract sum was 20,000,000 dollars. The owner wants to know what the termination itself cost, as distinct from scope he chose to add.

Step 1, total excess. 25,600,000 less 20,000,000 gives 5,600,000 dollars above the original contract.

Step 2, remove owner-chosen scope. The file shows 1,200,000 dollars of changes the owner instructed, which he would have paid for in any case. 5,600,000 less 1,200,000 leaves 4,400,000 dollars.

Step 3, split what remains by cause. The replacement contractor's premium on the remaining scope was 2,000,000 dollars. The original contractor's lost margin and demobilisation under the convenience conversion was 700,000. Legal and expert costs were 800,000. Delay was 900,000. Check: 2,000,000 plus 700,000 plus 800,000 plus 900,000 equals 4,400,000 dollars.

Step 4, ask which parts a clean process would have avoided. With proper notice and cure, the lost margin, most legal cost and part of the delay disappear; the replacement premium might remain if termination was still needed. On those assumptions, roughly 2,000,000 dollars of the 4,400,000 was the price of a defective process, and the rest was the price of a failing contractor.

Reverse two: the walk-away price for a negotiated exit

The outcome you want to beat: Roman's Day 3 comparison gave a properly documented termination an expected cost of about 2,150,000 dollars above contract. A negotiated exit, with releases, assigned subcontracts and a clean handover, carries a lower replacement premium, estimated at 1,500,000 dollars, because the new contractor inherits a documented site and the existing trades.

Step 1, start from the alternative. The negotiated exit is worth doing only if its total cost is below 2,150,000.

Step 2, subtract the costs the exit carries anyway. 2,150,000 less the 1,500,000 premium leaves 650,000 dollars.

Step 3, that is your ceiling. On these assumptions, any payment to the contractor below about 650,000 dollars for an agreed exit beats terminating. Above it, termination is cheaper in expectation, though riskier.

Step 4, adjust for certainty. A negotiated exit removes most of the dispute risk, so a sensible owner might pay close to the ceiling for that certainty, especially if the lender prefers it. Know the number before you sit down; Kema's Day 6 scene shows why.

Say that out loud now.

My walk-away price is the expected cost of my next best option, less the costs I carry either way.

Testing the walk-away price

A ceiling built on judgments needs a range, so move the two softest inputs. If counsel thinks the dispute risk on a termination is 60 percent rather than 40, the termination's expected cost rises by 0.2 times 1,000,000, or 200,000 dollars, to 2,350,000, and the ceiling rises to 850,000. If the bond recovery is less likely, say 30 percent rather than 50, expected recovery falls from 750,000 to 450,000, termination costs 2,450,000 and the ceiling rises to 950,000. If instead the negotiated exit's premium turns out to be 1,800,000 because the subcontractors will not stay, the ceiling falls to 350,000. So the honest statement is: on current judgments, a payment below roughly 350,000 to 950,000 dollars beats termination, and the input that moves it most is whether the key subcontractors will remain. That is the fact to establish before the meeting, by asking them.

Notice the discipline. The walk-away price is not a number you defend to the contractor. It is a number you defend to yourself, written down with its assumptions, so that the other side's opening offer cannot move it.

Reverse three: from the completion date to decision speed

The outcome: the building must reach substantial completion by a fixed date, because the construction loan matures shortly after and the buyers' closing conditions depend on it.

Step 1, find the float. The current schedule shows completion 20 working days before the required date. That is the float, the cushion the project has.

Step 2, reserve part of it for risks you cannot control. Your planner allows 8 working days for weather and supply. That leaves 12 working days that owner and design decisions may consume.

Step 3, count the decisions. The schedule shows 10 owner or design decisions still to come on the critical path.

Step 4, divide. 12 days over 10 decisions gives 1.2 working days per decision beyond the contract's allowed response time. If the contract allows 5 working days for a response, your average must stay at or below about 6.2 working days.

Step 5, set the target with margin. Set a target of 5 working days, the contractual time, and track it weekly. If the average drifts above 6, the completion date is at risk before anyone has missed a deadline on paper.

Notice how the three reverses fit together. Reverse three tells you how fast to decide to protect the date. Reverse two tells you what certainty is worth if the contractor fails. Reverse one tells you, afterwards, what your process cost you.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on every figure; construction lawyer, on the negotiated exit and termination assumptions; scheduler, on float and the decision count.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is negotiating an exit, or a recovery schedule, without a number in your head, so the other side's first offer becomes your anchor. The control is to calculate your walk-away price and your decision-speed target before the meeting.

The beginner's mistake

Reading a final account as one large number and concluding the contractor cost you everything. Decompose it. Some of it was your scope, some was the market, and some was your process. Only the last part is fully in your control next time, so it is the part to study hardest.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught the best alternative to a negotiated agreement and the reservation price. Reverse two is that idea in construction: the expected cost of termination is your alternative, and the walk-away price is your reservation price, calculated in advance and written down.

Recap

A 5,600,000 dollar overrun decomposed into 1,200,000 of chosen scope and 4,400,000 of termination cost, about half of it from a defective process. A negotiated exit beat termination below about 650,000 dollars. Twenty days of float, less eight for weather, over ten decisions set a decision target of about 5 working days.

Next: Kema on The Room: the conversation in which you deliver a notice of default.
checklist: I decompose any final account into chosen scope, market and process costs.
I compute the expected cost of my next best option before negotiating an exit.
I set a walk-away price in writing before the meeting.
I calculate the float available for owner and design decisions.
I count the remaining critical-path decisions and set a turnaround target.
I track my actual decision turnaround weekly against that target.
I have a quantity surveyor, lawyer and scheduler check each figure.
head: Field checklist
speak: Three reverse calculations, all hypothetical. First, a final account of 25,600,000 dollars on a 20,000,000 contract. Remove 1,200,000 of scope the owner chose, and 4,400,000 remains: a 2,000,000 replacement premium, 700,000 of lost margin, 800,000 of legal cost and 900,000 of delay, about half of it the price of a defective process. Second, the walk-away price for a negotiated exit: if a proper termination has an expected cost of 2,150,000 and a clean exit still carries a 1,500,000 premium, any payment below about 650,000 beats terminating. Third, from a fixed completion date: 20 days of float, less 8 for weather, leaves 12 for 10 critical-path decisions, so each may run only 1.2 days past the contract's 5-day window. Set the target at 5 and track it weekly.
terms: Final account — the agreed total of everything paid under a contract, including changes, claims and deductions.
Walk-away price — the most you will pay, or the least you will accept, in a negotiation, set from the value of your best alternative.
Float — the amount of time an activity, or the project, can slip without delaying a required date.

hostile.q: You offered the contractor 500,000 dollars to walk away. Why pay a failing contractor anything?
hostile.a: Because we priced the alternative. A properly documented termination has an expected cost of about 2,150,000 dollars above contract once the replacement premium, dispute risk and possible bond recovery are included. A negotiated exit with releases, assigned subcontracts and a clean handover carries a premium of about 1,500,000. On those figures, any exit payment below about 650,000 beats terminating, and it removes most of the dispute risk and protects the completion date the lender cares about. We are paying for certainty, below a ceiling we set before the meeting.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Delivering a Notice of Default
summary: A scene in which Mr Shabazz meets a contractor's principal to hand over a formal notice of default. Kema shows how to deliver it so that it protects every right and still gives the contractor a real chance to cure: the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent and how to hold your state.
body:
A notice of default is delivered calmly, with facts and a path to cure, because its purpose is either to fix the project or to make a later termination valid, and anger serves neither.

Recall

Q. State Rule 122.

A. Never terminate a contractor until the contract's notice, cure and certification steps are complete and documented, your own instructions are reconciled as changes and counsel has read the file; a termination is won or lost in the paper written months before it.

Q. On a benchmark tour, what do you do right after asking what the builder would change?

A. Stay silent, because the more honest answer often comes second.

Q. What is a factory acceptance test?

A. A test of equipment at the manufacturer's works, witnessed by the owner's representatives where required, before it is shipped, so that defects are found where they are cheapest to fix.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the hardest conversation in owner leadership, and the one most often handled badly. Most owners either avoid it until it is too late or deliver it in anger. Both cost money, as Ford and Roman showed. Done well, it is a short, clear, respectful meeting that leaves the contractor in no doubt and leaves you with every option open.

The scene

A hypothetical mid-rise job, 30 working days behind its baseline with no credible recovery plan, and staffing on site below the level the contractor committed to. Your lawyer has drafted the notice of default against the contract's clause: it names the failures, the clause and the cure period. It will be delivered formally by the method the notices clause requires; this meeting is a courtesy that accompanies it. You meet the contractor's principal in your office with your project manager. You have the notice, a one-page summary of the facts and your walk-away price for a negotiated exit in your head, not on the table.

Lines to say

"I want to tell you face to face before the formal notice arrives today. We are issuing a notice of default under the contract." Bottom line first, without preamble.

"The notice sets out three failures: the schedule is 30 working days behind with no recovery plan, site staffing is below the committed level, and two hold points were covered without release." Facts, countable, already documented.

"The contract gives you a cure period. I would like this job finished by you. What would a credible recovery plan need from you, and from us?" A real invitation, and the question about "from us" shows you have reconciled your own side.

"Let's meet again in one week, with your recovery plan, staffing and a revised schedule." A date, an agenda, a next step.

Say that out loud now.

We are issuing a notice of default. Here are the facts. The contract gives you a cure period. I would like you to finish this job.

Lines never to say

"You're fired." You are not, and saying it may be treated as repudiation.

"Everyone says your firm is in trouble." Gossip, which you cannot prove, and which may damage the firm with others.

"If you don't fix this I'll make sure nobody hires you again." A threat that adds nothing and may create a claim.

"Don't worry about the notice, it's just a formality." It is not, and if you say so, the contractor may later argue you waived it.

The question behind the question

When the principal says, "We've been waiting on your design answers," the question behind it is whether part of the delay is yours. You should already know, because you reconciled your own instructions and decision times before this meeting. Answer: "Some were late, and we've accounted for those in the notice. The remaining delay is in staffing and sequence." When he asks, "Are you going to terminate us?", the question behind it is whether there is a way back. Answer truthfully: "Not if the cure period produces a credible recovery. That's what I want."

If he raises the idea of an agreed exit, do not negotiate in this meeting. Say: "Let's see the recovery plan first. If it can't work, we can talk about other options." Your walk-away price stays in your head.

When to stay silent

After you state the three failures, stop. Let him respond. The first reaction is often anger or defence, and it passes faster if you do not argue with it. Stay silent again after you invite a recovery plan. What he offers in the next minute tells you whether a plan exists.

Holding your state

You will have rehearsed this, and you should. Before the meeting, while parked or sitting, a few slow breaths with a longer exhale steady most people; never do breathing drills while driving. Plant both feet, keep your hands still on the table and speak a little slower than feels natural. If he raises his voice, lower yours. If you feel yourself becoming defensive, return to the summary page and read the next fact aloud. The notice, not your tone, carries the authority.

Worked example: what you leave with

Hypothetical. Within an hour you write a short note to file, copied to counsel: the time and attendees, that the notice was explained and served formally, the principal's response in his own words, his claim that design answers were late and your reply, and the agreed meeting in one week for a recovery plan. You send the principal a brief email confirming the next meeting and its agenda, and nothing else. You tell the lender's monitor that a notice has been issued and that you expect a recovery plan within the cure period. And you ask your project manager to measure staffing on site daily for the next week. The file now shows a proper notice, a fair opportunity to cure and an owner acting calmly. Whatever happens next, that record works for you.

Time and energy on a shift schedule

This is a monthly thread, and it matters for meetings like this one. On a rotating shift schedule, your sharpest hours move every few days. Put conversations like this, and any decision with money or liability attached, on days when you are rested, ideally not the day after a night shift. Sleep loss tends to make people both more irritable and more willing to take risks, which is the worst combination in a confrontation. That is established research on sleep deprivation in general; how it applies to you is worth checking with your doctor.

Practically, keep a two-week calendar with your shifts in one colour and your project's fixed meetings in another, and move the hard meetings to your best days in advance. Leave the soft ones, site walks and routine updates, for the days you are tired. A system that respects your energy is as much part of leading as owner as the authority matrix.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting emotion turn a notice into a termination in the room, or into a threat that creates a claim. The control is a written script, the formal notice served separately by counsel, and a rule that you say nothing you would not want read aloud to a tribunal.

The beginner's mistake

Softening the notice so much in conversation that the contractor leaves believing it does not matter. Be kind in tone and exact in substance.

Callback

In Week 4, Kema taught slow breathing and stress reappraisal: reading a racing heart as readiness rather than threat. Today is the meeting that skill was built for. The physiology will arrive; your job is to name it, slow your breath while seated and let the facts do the work.

Recap

Deliver the notice face to face, bottom line first, with countable facts and a real path to cure. Never say fired, never threaten, never call it a formality. Hear the questions behind "your design answers" and "are you going to terminate", stay silent after the facts, schedule the meeting on a rested day and let the notice carry the authority.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: leading as owner, with a Red Pen drill on a notice of default.
checklist: I have counsel draft the notice against the contract's clause before the meeting.
I serve the notice formally by the method the notices clause requires.
I open with the bottom line and state countable, documented facts.
I reconcile my own instructions and decision delays before the meeting.
I invite a recovery plan and set a date for the next meeting.
I never say fired, threaten or call the notice a formality.
I keep my walk-away price in my head and do not negotiate an exit in this meeting.
I schedule hard meetings on rested days, not after a night shift.
head: Field checklist
speak: A notice of default is delivered calmly, because its job is either to fix the project or to make a later termination valid. Have counsel draft it against the contract's clause and serve it formally; the meeting is a courtesy that accompanies it. Open with the bottom line: we are issuing a notice of default. State countable facts: 30 working days behind with no recovery plan, staffing below commitment, two hold points covered without release. Say the contract gives a cure period and you would like them to finish the job, and ask what a recovery plan needs from them and from you. Never say fired, never threaten and never call it a formality. Stay silent after the facts. Know your walk-away price but do not negotiate an exit in the room. And schedule this meeting on a rested day, not after a night shift.
terms: Repudiation — conduct showing that a party will not perform its contract, which can entitle the other side to end it and claim damages.
Recovery plan — a contractor's written plan, with resources and a revised schedule, showing how it will regain lost time.
Stress reappraisal — interpreting the body's stress response as preparation for performance rather than as a threat.

hostile.q: You handed us a notice of default but you say you want us to finish. Which is it?
hostile.a: Both, and they are consistent. The notice records three documented failures and starts the cure period the contract gives you; it protects both of us by making the position clear. What I want is for you to use that period to bring a credible recovery plan, with staffing and a revised schedule, to our meeting next week. Where our own design answers were late, we have accounted for that. If the plan works, the notice will have done its job and the job continues. If it does not, we will follow the contract's next steps.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 122 Review: Leading as Owner
summary: Kema reviews leading as owner: the five-part operating system, the composite wrongful termination and Rule 122, the price of slow decisions and of each exit, the law of authority, notice and termination, the reverse calculations and the notice-of-default meeting. The Red Pen drill marks up a hypothetical notice of default.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: an owner leads through a written system of authority, cadence, escalation and accountability, and a termination is only as strong as the record that system has already built.

Recall

Q. In Roman's comparison, which exit from a failing contractor had the lowest expected cost?

A. The remedial plan, at about 1,500,000 dollars in expectation, because it was cheap if it worked and still led to a properly documented termination if it failed.

Q. In Week 120's Auditor's Chair, why was cutting contingency on the strength of a benchmark a defect?

A. Because an unverified benchmark should widen the range, not narrow it; the memo inverted the logic and rested on a sales conversation.

Q. Why does an owner care about the contractor's erection and installation sequence for prefabricated components?

A. Because sequence decides stability during construction, crane and hoist demand and when inspections can happen, so it drives both safety and the schedule.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the last teaching week of the phase on building it. Next comes the checkpoint. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can lead a construction project from the owner's chair with a system that survives a bad month. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the five parts of an owner's operating system.

Answer: Written authority through a delegation matrix, a fixed meeting cadence, an escalation ladder with time limits, accountability through one name and one date on every action, and termination as the documented last rung.

Question 2. State Rule 122.

Answer: Never terminate a contractor until the contract's notice, cure and certification steps are complete and documented, your own instructions are reconciled as changes and counsel has read the file; a termination is won or lost in the paper written months before it.

Question 3. What does an owner-caused critical-path delay cost, and what is the fix?

Answer: The project's daily carry for each day of delay: interest, the contractor's general conditions if compensable, and owner overheads. The fix is pushing decisions down within clear limits and escalating the few that matter on a clock, not working harder.

Question 4. What is the difference between actual and apparent authority?

Answer: Actual authority is what you really grant. Apparent authority is what your words or conduct reasonably lead a third party to believe someone has, which can bind you even if you never granted it.

Question 5. How do you set a walk-away price for a negotiated exit?

Answer: Take the expected cost of your next best option, usually a properly documented termination, subtract the costs the exit carries anyway, such as the replacement premium, and test the result as a range.

Question 6. What are the three things a notice of default should do?

Answer: Identify the specific failures, refer to the clause relied on and state the cure period, delivered by the method the notices clause requires.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco and Kema built the owner's operating system: authority, cadence, escalation, accountability and termination as the last rung. Ford and Cole took a composite owner who terminated by email after months of informal instructions, and wrote Rule 122. Roman priced decision latency and four exits from a failing contractor. LEX explained actual and apparent authority, notices, withholding and the two kinds of termination. Quincy worked backward from a final account, to a walk-away price and from a completion date to a decision target. Kema ran the notice-of-default meeting and the monthly thread on time and energy across a shift schedule.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical notice and find the defects before reading on.

From: owner's site manager. To: contractor's site foreman. Sent by text message, Friday 6:40 pm. Your performance has been unacceptable for months. Consider this formal notice of default. You have until Monday to fix everything or you are off the job. We are also holding this month's payment until further notice. Do not bother with excuses about our late drawings.

The defects. First, it is sent by someone outside the authority matrix, the site manager, to someone who probably cannot receive notices for the contractor, the foreman. Second, a text message is unlikely to meet the notices clause's required method and address. Third, it names no specific failure, only "performance", so the contractor cannot know what to cure. Fourth, it cites no clause. Fifth, "until Monday" is almost certainly not the contract's cure period, and a deadline shorter than the contract allows can make a later termination wrongful. Sixth, "off the job" reads as a threat of termination before the contract's steps are complete, which a contractor may treat as repudiation. Seventh, withholding payment "until further notice" without a contractual ground and the required withholding notice may itself put the owner in breach. Eighth, "do not bother with excuses about our late drawings" admits owner-caused delay in writing, which the contractor will cite in any delay claim.

The corrected version is a letter on company letterhead, signed by the named owner's representative, delivered by the method and to the address the notices clause requires, citing the clause, listing each failure against the baseline schedule and the contract's staffing and quality obligations, stating the contract's cure period, inviting a recovery plan by a stated date and saying nothing about payment unless counsel has confirmed a withholding ground and the notice for it. Counsel reviews it before it is sent.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "How do you actually control a construction project as owner?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Through a system, not by being on site. We issue an authority matrix at award, so everyone knows who can approve what and that other instructions do not bind us. We run a weekly owner-architect-contractor meeting and a monthly principals' meeting, with pre-reads, decisions recorded live and one name and one date on every action. Disagreements climb a ladder with time limits. We track our own decision speed, because every late owner decision on the critical path costs the daily carry. If a contractor fails, we price the options, a remedial plan, a negotiated exit or a proper termination, and we never terminate until the notice and cure steps are complete and counsel has read the file. The record we keep every week is what makes the hard decision safe when it comes."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name at least four parts of the system? Did you mention notice and cure before termination? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is that your own frustration, or your own people, act outside the system at the decisive moment: an informal instruction, a text-message notice, a payment withheld in anger. The control is a habit: every instruction through the matrix, every notice through counsel, every hard meeting on a rested day.

The beginner's mistake

Treating leadership as personality. Personality helps in the room; the system is what wins the dispute and finishes the building.

Callback

In Week 9, the first checkpoint, Kema asked you to record yourself explaining a hard idea and to score it for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question. You are about to do that again for this phase. Leading as owner is where those four scores matter most, because the owner's voice is the one the contractor, the lender and the tribunal all hear.

Recap

Authority written down, a fixed cadence, an escalation clock and one name on every action. Price your delays and your exits. Know whose instructions bind you and what a valid notice says. Deliver hard news calmly and on a rested day. Rule 122 makes termination the documented last rung, never a reaction.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was leading as owner. Lead through a system: an authority matrix issued at award, a weekly owner-architect-contractor meeting and a monthly principals' meeting with pre-reads and live decisions, an escalation ladder with time limits, and one name and one date on every action. Track your own decision speed, because owner-caused critical-path delay costs the daily carry. Know the law underneath: actual authority is what you grant, apparent authority is what your conduct implies, and a notice must name the failures, the clause and the cure period and go by the method the contract requires. When a contractor fails, price the exits, a remedial plan, a negotiated exit or a proper termination, and set a walk-away price in advance. Deliver a notice of default calmly, on a rested day. Rule 122: never terminate until notice, cure and certification are complete and counsel has read the file.
terms: Notices clause — the contract term setting how, to whom and where formal notices must be delivered to be valid.
Withholding notice — a written notice, often required before a payment falls due, stating an amount to be withheld and the reason.
Principals' meeting — a regular meeting of the senior people of each firm on a project, reviewing cost, schedule, risk and the relationship.

hostile.q: Your site manager texted our foreman a notice of default and said we were off the job by Monday. We are treating that as repudiation. What do you say?
hostile.a: That message was sent by someone without authority, by a method the contract does not recognise, and it does not reflect the owner's position. We withdraw it in writing today and confirm that the contract continues and that this month's payment will be processed in the normal way. We do have concerns about progress and staffing, and our representative will raise them through the contract, with a formal notice from counsel if needed, setting out specific failures and the cure period the contract gives you. I would rather we fix the schedule together than argue about a text message.
